content: Ambulatory anaesthesia is used for patients who are discharged on the same day as their surgery. It is critical to minimize perioperative complications such as postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), behavioural disturbances, and cardiorespiratory complications in this setting. The choice of anaesthetic agents and techniques can significantly influence the occurrence of these complications and may delay discharge. The objective of this review was to compare intravenous anaesthesia with inhalational anaesthesia in paediatric outpatient surgery, focusing on the risk of complications (PONV, behavioural disturbances, respiratory and cardiovascular complications) and recovery times (time to discharge from the recovery ward and hospital). The review included 16 randomized controlled trials involving 900 children. However, many studies did not adequately describe the randomization process or allocation concealment, and there was significant variability in the types and combinations of drugs used, as well as the duration of anaesthesia. This heterogeneity limited the ability to perform meta-analyses and interpret the results. For the induction and maintenance of anaesthesia, intravenous anaesthesia with propofol was associated with a lower incidence of PONV compared to inhalational anaesthesia with sevoflurane. Specifically, the incidence of PONV was 32.6% with sevoflurane and 16.1% with propofol (odds ratio [OR] 2.96; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.35 to 6.49; based on four studies with 176 children; low-quality evidence). Similarly, the risk of postoperative behavioural disturbances was lower with propofol (11.5%) compared to sevoflurane (24.7%) (OR 2.67; 95% CI 1.14 to 6.23; based on four studies with 176 children; very low-quality evidence). There were no significant differences between the two groups in terms of intraoperative and postoperative respiratory and cardiovascular complications (OR 0.75; 95% CI 0.27 to 2.13; based on three studies with 130 children; very low-quality evidence). Additionally, there was no difference in recovery time or time to discharge from the hospital. Two studies (105 participants) compared halothane to propofol and found conflicting results regarding the risk of PONV. There were no significant differences in the risks of intraoperative and postoperative complications between the groups. For the maintenance of anaesthesia, propofol (with or without nitrous oxide) was associated with a lower risk of complications compared to thiopentone or halothane combined with nitrous oxide (OR 3.23; 95% CI 1.49 to 7.02; based on four studies with 176 children; low-quality evidence; and OR 7.44; 95% CI 2.60 to 21.26; based on two studies with 87 children; low-quality evidence). For the time to discharge from the recovery room, no significant differences were observed between the groups. The studies included a variety of ambulatory surgeries and were associated with a high risk of bias. Four studies (250 participants) compared the induction of anaesthesia via the inhalational or intravenous route, with inhalational anaesthesia used for maintenance. These studies found no significant differences between the groups in terms of PONV, behavioural disturbances, respiratory and cardiovascular complications, or time to discharge from the recovery room. Due to significant clinical heterogeneity, a meta-analysis was not performed for this comparison. None of the included studies reported hospital readmissions or other adverse effects. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether intravenous anaesthesia with propofol reduces the risk of PONV and behavioural disturbances compared to inhalational anaesthesia in paediatric outpatient surgery. The evidence is of poor quality, and further high-quality studies are needed to compare different types of anaesthesia in various subsets of children undergoing ambulatory surgery.
